name: Meniscal Injury
summary: Traumatic or degenerative injury of the medial or lateral meniscus, presenting with joint-line pain, swelling and sometimes catching or locking.

tests.name: Thessaly Test
tests.purpose: Load the meniscus during weight-bearing rotation.
tests.positive: Reproduction of joint-line pain, catching or locking sensation.

tests.name: McMurray Test
tests.purpose: Assess meniscal symptom reproduction during rotation and knee motion.
tests.positive: Painful palpable/audible click or concordant joint-line pain.

stages.label: Symptom Control & Motion
stages.goal: Reduce irritability, regain extension/flexion and normalize gait.
do: Education about avoiding repeated provocative twisting early

stages.label: Strength & Control
stages.goal: Improve knee/hip strength and loaded movement.
moveOn: Tolerates stairs, squats and single-leg loading without locking or flare

stages.label: Higher Function
stages.goal: Restore running, pivoting or occupational demands.
when: Tolerates stairs, squats and single-leg loading without locking or flare
dose: 2–3 higher-level sessions/week with 24–48 h response monitoring

structures: Capsular attachments and adjacent cartilage may coexist
mechanism: Twisting on a flexed, weight-bearing knee
classification: Vertical/longitudinal, radial, horizontal, flap, root and complex tear patterns
investigations: MRI may be indicated for significant traumatic injury, persistent symptoms, surgical planning or diagnostic uncertainty.
Plain radiographs help assess OA or fracture when indicated.
manual: Joint mobilization can be used for coexisting ROM restriction.
Soft-tissue techniques may address secondary guarding but cannot 'move a torn meniscus back into place'.
Exercise and graded function remain central.
modalities: Ice/compression may help short-term symptom management.
Avoid relying on passive electrotherapy as the main treatment.
mistakes: Assuming every click equals a tear
Using a single special test as definitive
Avoiding all loading for too long
Missing a locked displaced tear requiring orthopaedic review
pearls: Joint-line pain + twisting mechanism + catching/locking raises suspicion.
True mechanical locking is different from pain-limited motion.

tests.name: Thessaly Test
tests.purpose: Load the meniscus during weight-bearing rotation.
tests.positive: Reproduction of joint-line pain, catching or locking sensation.
tests.patientPosition: Standing on the tested leg, usually with slight knee flexion; therapist provides support for balance.
tests.therapistPosition: In front of the patient, holding the hands/forearms for safety.
tests.handPlacement: Support through the patient's hands/forearms; no forced knee pressure.
procedure: Rotate body and knee internally and externally several times under control.
Stop if unstable or acutely painful.
tests.interpretation: Supports meniscal pathology; not diagnostic alone.

tests.name: McMurray Test
tests.purpose: Assess meniscal symptom reproduction during rotation and knee motion.
tests.positive: Painful palpable/audible click or concordant joint-line pain.
tests.patientPosition: Supine with hip and knee flexed.
tests.handPlacement: One hand controls the heel/tibia; the other palpates the joint line.
procedure: Fully flex the knee as tolerated.
Rotate the tibia while applying controlled valgus or varus bias.
Extend the knee while maintaining the rotational bias.
Repeat with the opposite rotational direction.
tests.interpretation: Supports meniscal injury when combined with history and other findings.

story.headline: The clicking knee: innocent sound or mechanical plot twist?
story.scene: A gardener twists while rising from a deep squat. His knee aches along the joint line. Every click is now described as 'the cartilage escaping.' Then he adds one detail: on one occasion the knee physically would not straighten.
story.dialogue: Patient: 'The click means my meniscus is gone, doesn't it?' Therapist: 'No. Knees are allowed to make sound effects. A truly locked knee is a different story.'
story.clue: Joint-line pain after twisting may fit meniscal pathology, but clicks alone have poor diagnostic value. Distinguish a true fixed extension block from motion limited by pain or fear.
story.twist: A displaced tear can cause true locking and needs timely specialist assessment. Many non-locked presentations improve with an individualized rehabilitation approach.
story.aha: A sound is not a diagnosis; the context and loss of function carry more weight.
story.patientTranslation: The shock-absorbing cartilage inside your knee may be irritated or injured. Clicking alone is common, but if the knee is genuinely stuck, that changes what we do next.
story.clinicianReasoning: Ask whether full extension is mechanically blocked. Screen trauma severity, effusion, ligament injury and OA. Use a cluster of history, examination and imaging/referral when appropriate; avoid using one McMurray or Thessaly result in isolation.
story.rehabBridge: When there is no urgent mechanical block: calm symptoms, restore extension and gait, strengthen the knee and hip, then reintroduce squats, turns and desired activities.
story.question: After a twist, a patient cannot fully extend the knee because it seems physically blocked. Your next move?
options: Force repeated deep squats to unlock it
Treat the click as harmless in all cases
Arrange timely medical/orthopaedic assessment for a truly locked knee
story.explanation: True mechanical locking may indicate a displaced meniscal tear or other intra-articular block and warrants prompt assessment rather than forceful exercises.
